blogs.title: CiliumCon is back at KubeCon + CloudNativeCon North America 2026
blogs.content: Posted on October 7, 2026 by Joe Stringer, Isovalent at Cisco & Jordan Rife, Google CNCF projects highlighted in this post Mark your calendars. On Monday, November 9, CilliumCon kicks off at KubeCon + CloudNativeCon North America in Salt Lake City. It’s the eighth time the event has run, and this year’s agenda goes straight at the problems that show up when AI and GPU workloads push Kubernetes networking past what it was built for. Why now? AI and GPU workloads are stretching Kubernetes networking, and this year’s CiliumCon agenda covers the problems that start to appear at that scale. Security is part of the story too. The same AI capabilities are changing the pace of vulnerability discovery, as models like Mythos have shown, and CVEs can now surface far faster than teams can patch them manually. That puts runtime security front and center, with Tetragon giving teams a way to detect and respond to threats as they happen. Where it all began CiliumCon began as a half-day co-located event at KubeCon + CloudNativeCon Europe 2023 in Amsterdam. It was created to give the growing Cilium community a dedicated space to connect, share production use cases, and align on technical roadmaps outside of the larger conference. It brings end users, maintainers, and contributors together to focus on production insights, eBPF enhancements, and community collaboration. Why CiliumCon? There’s no other event that goes as deep into Cilium, its sub-projects, and its eBPF foundation. One stack, one foundation. The whole Cilium stack runs on eBPF, with Cilium handling networking, Hubble observability, and Tetragon runtime security. Sessions build on that shared base instead of treating networking as a general topic. Built for scale. Cilium is the de facto CNI for the cloud native ecosystem, and as workload demand grows, users need to understand how to run it at scale and handle any new issues that come up. What’s on the agenda CiliumCon runs Monday, November 9, opening and closing with remarks from co-chairs Joe Stringer and Jordan Rife. In between, you’ll hear from end users and maintainers: ESnet on IPv6-only ClusterMesh OpenAI on debugging inference workloads with eBPF Datadog on a fleet-wide netkit migration Maintainer-led technical sessions on sidecarless mTLS and multi-cluster networking Cloud native themes CiliumCon lines up with two cloud native themes: Cloud Native AI and Security . Cloud Native AI: Several sessions deal directly with networking and security constraints specific to AI and GPU workloads, from IPv6 addressing to RDMA policy enforcement to debugging inference traffic. Security: The security sessions cover enforcement in the kernel, from sidecarless mTLS that authenticates pod traffic without app changes to Tetragon’s runtime policies. These matter more as vulnerabilities surface faster and AI clusters need the same isolation as any other workload. What you’ll walk away with You’ll leave with practical approaches to problems many teams haven’t hit yet, including: Running Kubernetes on IPv6 only What actually breaks during a large-scale CNI datapath migration Enforcing network policy on RDMA traffic for AI clusters Tracing packet loss in latency-sensitive workloads with eBPF These takeaways come from real production use, so you’ll go home with real strategies you can put to work. Who should come? Platform and infrastructure engineers running Cilium, Hubble, or Tetragon in production. You’ll get the most out of it, especially if you’re weighing a CNI migration or networking changes to support AI workloads. Engineers evaluating Cilium for the first time. Get an honest account of what adoption involves, plus tips and tricks from people who have already solved similar problems. Contributors. Get face time with maintainers. A working knowledge of Kubernetes networking and container orchestration is enough for most sessions. A few of the more advanced talks assume familiarity with specific Cilium features (ClusterMesh, netkit, existing NetworkPolicy behavior). Newcomers can get up to speed with the eBPF documentary, the Buzzing Across Space children’s guide to eBPF and its Cilium follow-up Buzzing Beyond Clouds, or Learning eBPF by Liz Rice. Come meet the community At CiliumCon, users get to tell maintainers what broke in production, and maintainers get to explain why it works the way it does, without waiting on a GitHub issue thread. It’s also an easy way for new contributors to meet maintainers in person, ask about a PR or a design decision, and put faces to the GitHub handles they’ve been working with. Join us at CiliumCon on Monday morning, November 9, 2026, in Salt Lake City, as part of KubeCon + CloudNativeCon North America 2026. Register Now Share

blogs.title: BackstageCon comes to KubeCon + CloudNativeCon North America 2026 in Salt Lake City
blogs.content: Posted on October 7, 2026 by BackstageCon CNCF projects highlighted in this post BackstageCon takes place all day on Monday, November 9, 2026, the day before KubeCon + CloudNativeCon North America opens in Salt Lake City. We’re excited to bring together Backstage adopters, contributors, and maintainers to share how teams have used Backstage in practice, including the AI features the project has been shipping for the past year. ne project, one track, one full day with the people who actually run it. AI is changing the game. Where does your portal fit? AI is changing how teams build software. If you’re already running Backstage, you probably want to know where your developer portal fits now. If you’re just getting started, you want to make the most of it while AI becomes part of everyday work. The Backstage project has been shipping AI features for the past year. BackstageCon is where you hear how teams have really used them and meet others working through the same problems. Where it all began The first BackstageCon took place in Detroit in October 2022, co-located with KubeCon + CloudNativeCon North America. It was the first official Backstage conference, and it started after the Backstage project approached the CNCF. It has returned regularly since. The reason is simple. Backstage was growing fast, with more adopters and more contributors, but there was nowhere for the community to meet in person. BackstageCon gave adopters, contributors, and maintainers a place to connect and swap stories. Why spend a whole day on Backstage? The main KubeCon schedule has one or two Backstage talks. BackstageCon gives the project a full day, so you can go far deeper. Real-world stories. Most sessions come from adopters talking about what they’ve done in production. One track, one conversation. Users, contributors, and maintainers all see the same talks, so by the time the hallway chats start, everyone has plenty to talk about. The bigger picture. Backstage usually sits on top of a Kubernetes and cloud native stack, and BackstageCon shows how platform teams make that stack usable for their developers. What’s on the agenda It’s a single track of breakout sessions and lightning talks, from opening remarks to closing remarks, with breaks along the way for networking. Sessions fall into four tracks: AI agents and context in Backstage Technical deep dives Developer experience and workflows Lessons learned from deploying Backstage and driving adoption Every talk is labeled beginner, intermediate, or any level, so you can pick the sessions that match where you are with Backstage. What you’ll walk away with You’ll leave with ideas you can try in your own Backstage instance, taken from teams who have already done the work. Talks cover: Bringing AI agents into Backstage while keeping people in the loop Giving those agents the right identity and permissions Automating catalog ownership Keeping plugins current as the project changes One session makes the case that the hardest parts of adoption are about people, not technology. You’ll also get a look at where Backstage is heading, including how one team used AI to modernize a Backstage instance that’s been running for a decade. Who should come? Platform teams running Backstage in production. You’ll probably get the most out of it. Many speakers are wrestling with the same problems at scale, like catalog ownership and adding AI to their portals. Teams evaluating Backstage or early in adoption. Learn from organizations that are further along. Several sessions are aimed at beginners. Contributors and plugin authors. See where the project is going and meet maintainers in person. No prep is required. If you’re new to Backstage, it helps to skim the documentation first, especially the Software Catalog, Software Templates, and plugins, since many talks assume you know those. A lot of the schedule covers AI agents and MCP, so a basic understanding of the Model Context Protocol will help too. Come meet the community BackstageCon is where the Backstage community meets in person. You’ll hear how others use the project and share your own experience, whether you started last month or have run it for years. Attendees regularly leave with new ideas and with people they keep talking to long after the event. It’s also a great chance to meet maintainers and contributors, which makes getting involved much easier. Join BackstageCon on November 9, 2026, in Salt Lake City, as part of KubeCon + CloudNativeCon North America 2026. Register Now for KubeCon + CloudNativeCon NA! Share

blogs.title: Kubernetes on Edge Day returns to KubeCon + CloudNativeCon North America 2026
blogs.content: Posted on October 7, 2026 by Mars Toktonaliev and Katerina Arzhayev, Kubernetes on Edge Day CNCF projects highlighted in this post Kubernetes on Edge Day returns to KubeCon + CloudNativeCon North America 2026 on November 9 in Salt Lake City, Utah, bringing together developers and adopters from across the cloud native ecosystem to share experiences and insights around building, improving, and operating edge infrastructure. As hardware and software are distributed across hundreds or even thousands of locations, cloud native approaches to observability, loosely coupled systems, declarative APIs, and strong automation become increasingly relevant. Kubernetes is already an important part of the edge ecosystem, and Kubernetes on Edge Day creates a dedicated space for the community to explore the intersection of cloud native and edge computing. From cloud native to the edge Kubernetes on Edge Day first launched as a co-located event at KubeCon + CloudNativeCon Europe in Valencia, Spain, in 2022. Since then, the event has grown alongside an ecosystem in which Kubernetes is increasingly being considered and deployed beyond traditional data centers and public clouds. The event was created to address the gap between traditional, data-center-centric cloud native approaches and the operational realities of edge computing. Running Kubernetes across distributed and resource-constrained environments introduces challenges that can differ considerably from centralized cloud environments. Hardware and software may be spread across many locations, resources may be constrained, and connectivity cannot always be treated in the same way as it is in a conventional data center or public cloud environment. Kubernetes on Edge Day provides a dedicated space for the community to discuss these challenges and share approaches to applying cloud native technologies in edge environments. Why Kubernetes on Edge Day? KubeCon + CloudNativeCon covers a broad spectrum of Kubernetes and cloud native technologies. Kubernetes on Edge Day focuses specifically on what happens when those technologies are applied at the edge. What to expect Kubernetes on Edge Day is a CNCF-hosted co-located event taking place on November 9, 2026, at KubeCon + CloudNativeCon North America in Salt Lake City. The focus is on the intersection between Kubernetes, cloud native technologies, and edge computing, providing an opportunity for attendees to learn from the experiences of others working in distributed environments and to participate in the broader community conversation around cloud native at the edge. Cloud native themes Kubernetes on Edge Day intersects with several areas of cloud native computing. Observability and Security are particularly relevant themes for edge environments. Observability is an important consideration when hardware and software are distributed across many locations. The cloud native approaches that have helped operators understand and manage distributed systems in the cloud are also relevant as infrastructure moves toward the edge. Security is similarly important as cloud native workloads and infrastructure operate across increasingly distributed environments. Edge deployments introduce their own operational conditions, making security an important part of the wider discussion about how Kubernetes and cloud native technologies are used outside traditional data centers. What can attendees take away? Attendees can expect to leave with a clearer understanding of the technical and operational considerations involved in using Kubernetes and cloud native technologies at the edge. The event provides an opportunity to learn from practitioners working with distributed infrastructure, understand the challenges they encounter, and explore how cloud native principles such as automation, declarative management, and observability can apply in edge environments. It also gives attendees a broader view of how the Kubernetes and cloud native communities are approaching edge computing and where further collaboration and technical work may be needed. Who should attend? Kubernetes on Edge Day is relevant to developers and adopters interested in deploying Kubernetes and cloud native technologies at the edge, as well as practitioners already working with distributed infrastructure. Platform engineers, infrastructure architects, operators, developers, and others responsible for environments outside traditional data centers or public clouds may find the discussions particularly useful. The event can also provide useful context for newcomers who want to better understand the relationship between Kubernetes, cloud native technologies, and edge computing. A foundational understanding of Kubernetes, containers, and distributed systems can help attendees follow more technical discussions, but the event also provides an opportunity to learn directly from members of the community working on edge infrastructure. Strengthening the community Kubernetes on Edge Day creates a space for people working across cloud native and edge computing to exchange knowledge and experiences. Bringing developers, adopters, operators, and other practitioners together helps surface common challenges and provides opportunities to share approaches to building and improving edge infrastructure. As Kubernetes continues to be used beyond traditional data centers and public clouds, this community exchange can help practitioners learn from one another and contribute to the ongoing evolution of cloud native technologies at the edge. Join Kubernetes on Edge Day on November 9, 2026, in Salt Lake City, Utah, as part of KubeCon + CloudNativeCon North America 2026. Share
